questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had long been certain that I wanted to study in an English-speaking country, as this would eliminate any language barriers and ensure that all instruction was in a language I fully understood. I applied to several universities in both the United States and the United Kingdom, but ultimately chose Boston as my first priority for several reasons. First, I wanted to experience life in the United States firsthand. Second, I had heard that Boston is an exceptional city to live in, particularly for students. Finally, I found many of the courses offered there to be especially interesting and well aligned with my academic interests.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I truly valued my study abroad experience. While certain aspects—particularly the social side—were more challenging than I had initially anticipated, this is why I have not rated the experience a full ten. Nevertheless, I gained a great deal from the experience, both academically and in terms of personal growth. I would strongly recommend that anyone who is even considering studying abroad take the opportunity, as it is without a doubt a highly rewarding and worthwhile experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The process was very straightforward. Boston University provided extensive information before the start of the semester, including an online course for all new BU students that introduced the university, available opportunities, and resources for support. In addition, there was a separate online course specifically for international students, which explained what to expect in the United States, including the grading system, how classes are structured, and even appropriate ways to address professors. The exchange program manager was also very proactive in sharing clear and helpful information both prior to the semester and during its initial weeks.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: In addition to the information mentioned above, there was an introductory week for all new students at the university. During this week, international students were grouped together, which provided an opportunity to meet one another. The program included both social events and more practical sessions, such as introductions to the university and its facilities. Overall, I found the introductory week somewhat confusing and not particularly helpful, largely because it was primarily designed for students beginning their full degree at the university rather than exchange students. That said, the meeting with the exchange program manager was very helpful. I would have appreciated a more thorough campus tour and additional social time with other exchange students. However, I did not feel that I began the semester lacking any crucial information or feeling overwhelmed, which was reassuring.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Finding housing was quite challenging, primarily because it was difficult to secure accommodation for only four months. Most rental properties in Boston operate with one-year leases, which significantly limited the available options. That said, there are many Facebook groups dedicated to people searching for apartments or rooms in Boston, though it is important to be cautious. I nearly signed a lease with someone who initially appeared to be a very friendly landlord, but after searching her name online, I discovered that she was well known in Boston for being a problematic landlord and a scammer.
The university also offers a platform for students seeking off-campus housing, where it is possible to find roommates. I ultimately found a roommate through this platform who already had an apartment and was looking to share it. While securing housing is certainly possible, the process can be stressful and requires patience and diligence.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
One important detail I wish I had known before applying to the exchange program at BU is that students aged 26 or older are not permitted to live on campus. Students under this age are generally guaranteed on-campus housing. As I was 27 at the time, I was required to find off-campus housing.
Initially, this was quite discouraging, and I even considered withdrawing from the exchange program. However, I eventually found an apartment shared with two other people and ended up being very satisfied with the arrangement - particularly because the monthly rent was significantly lower than on-campus housing. I paid approximately $1,100 per month, whereas dormitory housing typically costs $2,000 or more.
That said, living off campus does mean missing out on some of the social aspects of campus life, which can make it more challenging to form friendships. For this reason, it is important to consider personal priorities when deciding whether on-campus or off-campus housing is the better option.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Regarding my overall rating of the housing available to students, I rated it a 1. As mentioned above, I was not eligible for on-campus housing due to my age, and I was not made aware that this was a possibility until around June, despite the program starting in September. I would have greatly appreciated having this information prior to applying. Based on the lack of transparency surrounding housing eligibility - and, to some extent, the fact that I was not permitted to live on campus - I felt that a rating of 1 was appropriate.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Before course registration opens, students have access to an online portal that lists all available courses, including detailed descriptions and any prerequisite requirements. The portal also includes a “schedule builder” feature, which allows students to add courses they are interested in and see how they fit together in a potential timetable.
When registration opens, courses are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis. It is therefore important to register promptly, particularly as full-time degree students are given priority access, which can limit the number of available spots. If a course is full at the time of registration, it is possible to join a waitlist.
Many students adjust their schedules or drop courses before or during the beginning of the semester, meaning that being on a waitlist is not without hope. I was personally on the waitlist for three courses and was ultimately admitted to all of them.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
Before registration opened, all exchange students participated in an online meeting with the exchange program manager, during which she explained the registration system very thoroughly. This included guidance on how to register, how many courses we were allowed to take, and common mistakes students often make during the registration process.
She was also readily available by email to answer any questions related to registration, including on the day registration opened, when she responded within minutes.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Many of the courses I had initially planned to take, based on my early research into the university’s offerings, were ultimately not available during that semester. In that respect, I was not successful in registering for the specific courses I had originally intended to pursue.
However, once I reviewed the courses that were actually offered, I was able to register for all of the classes I selected. In that sense, the registration process was ultimately successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
It is important to keep in mind that even if a course is listed as usually being offered in a specific semester, this does not guarantee that it will actually be available. I found several courses on BU’s website that were indicated as being offered in both the fall and spring semesters, but when registration opened, many of these courses were not available during the fall semester when I was there. If you have particular courses you are especially interested in, it may therefore be worthwhile to contact the university in advance to confirm their availability.
Additionally, it is important to note that the U.S. system allows students to change courses at the beginning of the semester. For example, after the first week, I realized that one course was not what I had expected and was able to drop it and enroll in another instead. It is also possible to register for more courses than required initially, which allows you to explore different options before finalizing your schedule.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I greatly appreciated how specialized the courses are in the United States. In my experience, many courses at KU are quite broad, particularly because 15 ECTS courses need to cover a wide range of material. While there were some introductory courses at Boston that were similarly broad, most courses were closely aligned with the professors’ specific fields of research.
This approach ensures that instructors are experts in the topics they teach and allows their enthusiasm for the subject to be clearly reflected in the classroom. It also makes it possible to engage deeply with a subject and explore it in detail, which I found both rewarding and enjoyable.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
In my personal experience the courses are neither harder nor easier at Boston University than at Copenhagen University. 
But the teaching style, described below, is very different and that can make it feel harder, especially in the beginning. Although I initially found this teaching style intimidating, I ultimately came to appreciate it, as it fostered a highly engaged and well-prepared learning environment. However, the continuous stream of assignments, quizzes, and assessments throughout the semester, in addition to regular readings, also meant that I had significantly less free time than I had expected. For students who place a strong emphasis on achieving high grades, it is important to be prepared for a heavier and more consistent workload throughout the semester compared to KU, where the most intensive work typically takes place during the exam period.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching style at Boston University differs significantly from that at KU. In my experience, there is a much stronger emphasis on participation at Boston University. In all of the courses I took, the final grade was composed of multiple smaller assessments, including assignments, presentations, quizzes, class participation, and in some cases a final exam. Attendance was often factored into the overall grade, which created a clear incentive to attend classes regularly.
The focus on participation also led to far more in-class discussions than I was accustomed to at KU. Rather than primarily listening to a professor lecture, classes frequently involved active dialogue, with professors posing questions and, at times, allowing discussions to take up most of the session. Because participation was graded, there was a strong motivation to prepare for class and complete the assigned readings—something most students consistently did.

questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all my courses, but especially Sexuality in ancient Greece and Rome. The subject was fascinating and professor Smith was so knowledgeable and enthusiastic about the topic.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs. I went on a lot of trips to other places in New England which is not part of the budget above.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food is a difficult category. I was not shy about going out to restaurants or ordering take out. While groceries are expensive my food budget would probably have been lower if I ate more home cooked meals. 
Also, my food budget is based on me living of campus. Most people living on campus don't have a kitchen and are instead required to buy a meal plan for the dining halls. I also bought a meal plan, but it was a cheaper one designed for students living off campus who just want to eat a few meals in the dining halls.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are over 400 clubs at Boston University, including academic clubs, sports clubs, cultural/religious clubs and clubs for different hobbies. There are clubs like the school newspaper, model UN, debate, board games, Dungeons and Dragons, rocket Science and so on.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I was part of the Classics Association and the History Club. For all international students I would recommend the international dinners held weekly in the basement of Marsh Chapel, the church on Campus. It is a great place to meet other intentional students and you don't have to be religious to join (I wasn't).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Boston is an amazing city, especially if you like American history. There are so many historic sites related to the American Revolution in Boston and the surrounding area. I would definitely recommend doing the Freedom Trail. Are you there in the fall, then I would also recommend doing a foliage tour in the White Mountains. I would also advise people to explore the rest of Massachusetts, for example Cape Cod. I went to both Plymouth and Nantucket and would recommend both places. Salem is also a must see. And go watch a Red Sox game!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. Boston is probably the most European city in the US.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
It is very hard. In my experience Americans love small talk, but it is hard to get closer to them than that and actually form a real connection. It is also my experience that some American students aren't interested in getting to know exchange students because we aren't there very long. I literally had a local student tell me that it wasn't worth the effort getting to know me because I would be leaving in a few months. 
The easiest place to socialize with local students are at the clubs. It can be hard to find time to talk to people during class, but if you join some clubs you are sure to meet American students who share your interests. 
Again, my experience is based on me living off campus. It might be easier if you live near the local students. Though most international people I have talked to share my experience and I know most exchange students living on campus end up living with other exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Other than the social aspect explained above and the teaching style explained further above, nothing was that challenging. But remember that Boston and the US is a lot more dangerous than Denmark. There are definitely parts of Boston that you should not go to at night.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
Looking back, I greatly appreciated how proud Bostonians are of their city. People take genuine pride in Boston’s history, food culture, sports teams, and its many unique quirks. While this pride might initially seem intense or even slightly nationalistic, what stood out most to me was how willingly and enthusiastically they shared their city with others.
Rather than conveying a sense of exclusivity, the attitude was very much one of openness - an eagerness to welcome others and invite them to experience what makes the city special. This enthusiasm is contagious, and it does not take long before you begin to share in that pride yourself. Overall, it creates a warm and welcoming atmosphere that makes you feel truly included.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1: Are you 26 or older you cannot live on campus
2: The teaching style is very different and can be hard to get used to
3: Boston is an amazing city. I fell in love with it immediately and it will always have a special place in my heart.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The academic program and experiencing Boston.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The social aspect.

Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
